sentences.text: Dacentrurus means "tail full of points" and is an extinct stegosaurian dinosaur from Europe living between 154 and 140 million years ago.
It is one of the largest known stegosaurs, reaching lengths of 8 to 9 meters and weights of up to 7.4 metric tons.
Specimens reached 8 to 9 meters in length, 1.8 meters in hip height, and 5 to 7.4 metric tons in body mass.
The generic name Dacentrurus derives from the Greek word for "upper arm", referring to its robust humerus.
This dinosaur had a massive humerus with an enormous deltopectoral crest that served as an attachment for powerful musculature.
Dacentrurus had a small head with a flattened beak and aligned molars on both sides for crushing plants.
A 125-millimetre-long egg attributed to Dacentrurus represents the first egg ever associated with any stegosaur.
The preserved tail spike in the holotype has a maximum length of 456 millimetres.
The holotype includes a small, blunt, asymmetrical plate on the neck or front back.
Richard Owen named and described the type species in 1875 as Omosaurus armatus.
The type species Omosaurus armatus was named in 1875 based on a skeleton found in England.
The genus Dacentrurus was established by Lucas in 1902.
The genus name was changed to Dacentrurus in 1902 because Omosaurus was already in use for a phytosaur.
Dacentrurus was the first stegosaur known from articulated remains and became the default classification for most European stegosaur finds.
Richard Owen described Dacentrurus armatus in 1875 as the first known stegosaur.
The holotype skeleton lacks the skull and consists only of postcranial elements.
Large olecranon horns on the ulnae and large deltoid crests on the humerus suggest a powerful deltoid muscle capable of strong flexion and abduction.
Dacentrurus likely used its anchored forelimbs and sweeping tail thagomizer to defend against large theropods like Torvosaurus.
Edwin Hennig moved several Omosaurus species into Dacentrurus in 1915, creating multiple species within the genus.
Several species originally assigned to Dacentrurus were later reclassified, including D. durobrivensis (now Lexovisaurus durobrivensis), D. phillipsi, and D. vetustus (now Lexovisaurus vetustus).
Studies in 2008 and 2010 determined that Dacentrurus forms the clade Dacentrurinae with Miragaia longicollum as its sister species.
The parent group of the genus Dacentrurus is the subfamily Dacentrurinae.
Dacentrurus was the first stegosaurid with good remains discovered, whereas earlier finds like Paranthodon, Regnosaurus, and Craterosaurus were too limited to be recognized as a distinct new group.
Dacentrurus lived approximately 145 million years ago during the Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary and was prevalent in the Iberian range.
Dacentrurus armatus lived during the late Jurassic period, approximately 157 to 152 million years ago, in what is now Europe.
Fossil evidence of this dinosaur is found throughout Europe, including England, France, Spain, and five skeletons found in Portugal.
The genus Dacentrurus lived from the Kimmeridgian to the Barremian, between 154.8 and 121.4 million years ago.
Some researchers suggest that Miragaia longicollum is a junior synonym of Dacentrurus armatus.
The limited fossil record makes the appearance of Dacentrurus uncertain and its relationships with other stegosaurs contentious.
It is debated whether material from the Villar del Arzobispo Formation belongs to Dacentrurus or Miragaia, as 2019 research showed stronger affinities to Miragaia.
It is debated whether Dacentrurus is a basal or derived stegosaurid, with later analyses showing it to be relatively derived.
It is currently undetermined whether Dacentrurus actually possessed a shoulder spike similar to Kentrosaurus.
In 2008, Susannah Maidment adopted a radically different approach by limiting the material of D. armatus to its holotype.
